phonemes.desc: Voiceless unaspirated bilabial stop [p]; the rough breathing is absent in the Greek spelling.
Close front vowel [y], like French 'tu', with acute stress.
Aspirated voiceless dental stop [tʰ], distinct from English 'th'.
Long open-mid back rounded vowel [ɔː], marked by the macron/circumflex.

pronunciation.approximation: 'PYOO-thohn' — round the lips for 'pyoo', then aspirate the 'th' as in 'top-hon', and hold the final vowel long.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Πύθων (Pýthōn), the serpent of Delphi and the name of the place itself.

kin.label: Delphi
kin.form: Pythō, an old name for the sanctuary, from the verb pýthein, 'to rot'.

kin.label: Modern confusion
kin.form: The name was later borrowed for a programming language via Monty Python's Flying Circus; the deity has no connection to it.

pronunciation.note: Pýthōn is Tier 1: the Greek original carries both acute stress and a long vowel (ō). The English 'Python' flattens both features.

domains.title: Serpent of Delphi
domains.subtitle: Chthonic Oracle, Slain by Apollo
domains.lead: Pýthōn is the primeval she-serpent who guarded the oracular sanctuary at Delphi. Born from the slime after the flood, she coiled around the omphalos, the navel-stone of the world, until the young Apollo descended from Olympus and slew her. From her corpse the sanctuary took its name, and the Pythia priestess took hers.

cards.name: Guardian of the Oracle
cards.desc: She protected the chthonic oracle of Gaia at Delphi before Apollo's arrival.

cards.name: Earth Dragon
cards.desc: A child of the Earth, she embodies the earth's primitive, prophetic power.

cards.name: Defeat by Apollo
cards.desc: Apollo's victory over her marks the ascendancy of Olympian prophecy over chthonic earth religion.

cards.name: Pythian Games
cards.desc: The great festival at Delphi commemorated her death with athletic and musical contests.

symbols.name: Serpent/dragon
symbols.meaning: The chthonic power that must be subdued before Apollo can rule Delphi.

symbols.name: Omphalos
symbols.meaning: The navel-stone of the world around which she coiled.

symbols.name: Laurel
symbols.meaning: The plant sacred to Apollo, whose victory over Pýthōn established Delphi's laurel cult.

symbols.name: Tripod
symbols.meaning: The seat of the Pythia priestess who inherited Pýthōn's prophetic voice.

mythology.lead: The myth of Pýthōn is the myth of Apollo's coming-of-age: a young god must kill the ancient serpent to claim his prophetic throne — and then, characteristically, must explain the killing away.

myths.title: Born from the Deluge's Slime
myths.text: When Zeus ended the age of bronze with a flood, the receding waters left the world coated in black mud. From that slime the Earth brought forth Pýthōn, a monstrous serpent (Hyginus, Fabulae 140; the fullest archaic account is the Homeric Hymn to Apollo 300–306, where she is a drakaina, a she-dragon — later authors vary her gender). She made her lair in the gorge below Parnassus, at the springs, and held the place against gods and men: a pre-Olympian wardress of the earth's oldest oracle, born of the world's rot and guarding its secrets. The sources make her terrible but not wicked — a boundary-keeper, not a tempter. What the flood kills does not vanish, the myth whispers; it sinks into the mud, coils around the springs, and waits for whoever comes to claim the holy place.

myths.title: Apollo Descends to Delphi
myths.text: Apollo came down from Olympus to claim a sanctuary, and the serpent was in his way. The Homeric Hymn to Apollo (300–374) tells it with glee: the young god strung his silver bow — the one even Zeus does not disdain — and his first arrows went into the monster's breast. She crashed down the ravine, writhing, fouling the spring with her gore, and there she rotted under the sun: pýthein, 'to rot', is the verb the Greeks heard in her name, and so the place was called Pythô. Ovid's brief retelling (Metamorphoses 1.438–451) complains that a thousand arrows were barely enough for so vast a bulk. Apollo then built his altar and temple above the corpse and set his tripod over the chasm. The myth's economy is exact: a single body gives the sanctuary both its name and its legitimacy, and the god's new oracle rises, quite literally, on top of the old one.

myths.title: The Oracle Passes Down
myths.text: Greek conscience needed the killing explained, and Aeschylus supplies the genealogy of excuses. In the opening of the Eumenides (1–8) the Pythia herself recites the succession: first Gaia held the oracle; then Themis received it; then Phoibe, daughter of Earth, took it — and Phoibe gave it to Phoibos Apollo as a birthday gift, who thus bears the name of his maternal forebear. An inheritance, not a conquest: Apollo's title rests on a chain of custody running back to the Earth herself. The Homeric Hymn adds a comic rehearsal of the same anxiety — before Delphi, Apollo was first lured toward the spring of Telphousa, whose nymph tried to keep the glory for herself by warning him of the local dragon; the god saw through the trick, slew Pýthōn, and took her spring's glory anyway. The tradition insists: even a righteous slayer must show his title-deeds, and the oracle's legitimacy is only as old as its paperwork.

myths.title: The Woman on the Tripod
myths.text: The slain serpent's office passed to a woman. On a tripod above the chasm at Delphi sat the Pythia — a priestess of Apollo who inherited Pýthōn's very title — uttering the god's answers while the sanctuary hummed around her: the Castalian spring, the omphalos stone, the laurel she held, the cauldron over the fissure in the rock. How the trance worked was debated even in antiquity; Plutarch reports sober and ecstatic versions (On the Obsolescence of Oracles), and modern geology has added a third — analysis of Delphi's spring waters has detected light hydrocarbon gases able to induce altered states in an enclosed chamber (de Boer, Hale, and Chanton, Geology 29, 2001). Every four years the Pythian Games crowned victors where the corpse had lain. The serpent's name could not be killed: every priestess who ever sat the tripod answered, by title, to the dragon Apollo slew — the victim's name outliving the victor's arrows.

lore.syncretism: Pýthōn belongs to the oldest stratum of myth: the dragon of the deep waters slain by the newcomer god, a pattern running from Tiamat through Vṛtra to Leviathan — the chaos-battle the comparatists mapped, here shrunk to a single gorge in Phocis. Her gender was disputed even in antiquity — female (drakaina) in the Homeric Hymn, male in Hyginus and Ovid — and the wavering suits her: earth-mother's child and storm-god's victim, oracle and obstacle, the power that must be defeated before truth can speak. Christian writers, less ambivalent, read her as the devil's kin, and the serpent guarding the shrine became, in their telling, the serpent of Eden in local dress.
lore.culturalLegacy: Pýthōn lives on in the Pythian Games, the Pythia priestess, and the very word 'python' — borrowed first by a British comedy troupe and then by a programming language that took its name from the circus, not the serpent, though its two-snake logo restores the reptile by the back door. More seriously, the myth remains a foundational text for understanding how Apollo's rational prophecy superseded older, chthonic forms of divination: every oracle of Delphi still stands in the shadow of the serpent he killed. The Christian centuries kept her too — the slave-girl of Philippi possessed by a 'spirit of Python' (Acts 16:16) gave the languages of Europe the word pythoness for any woman who tells fortunes.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Pýthōn is the past that must be killed before the future can speak. She is the old oracle, the earth's own voice, the serpent wisdom that predates Olympus. Apollo does not deny her power; he inherits it. The Pythia sits where the serpent coiled; the tripod replaces the coils.

There is something honest in this myth. New institutions rarely arise from empty ground. They come by confronting, incorporating, and renaming what came before. To remember Pýthōn is to remember that every 'new' revelation has an older voice behind it, and that the name of the defeated often outlasts the name of the victor — the sanctuary is called Pythô after her, and her title became her killer's priestess.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Greek is Πύθων, connected by the ancients with the verb πύθω ('to rot'), because the serpent's corpse decayed at Delphi. The initial Π is the unaspirated stop [p] — breathings occur only on initial vowels and rho, never on a consonant — while the theta of the second syllable is the aspirated stop [tʰ] that Latin script writes 'th'. The acute on ύ marks the pitch peak, and the final -ων is long. PUNICODEX writes Pýthōn with the acute and the macron on the long vowel, the two features the domain system can carry.

sources.name: Plutarch, On the Obsolescence of Oracles

lore.archaeology: The site itself is the monument: French excavations at Delphi (from 1892) uncovered the successive temples of Apollo, the great altar, the Castalian spring, and the omphalos, whose carved net-pattern marks the 'navel-stone' the serpent was said to guard. The myth had a long life in art: sixth- and fifth-century Attic vases — lekythoi and drinking cups especially — show the coiled drakaina taking Apollo's arrows beside the tripod, making the slaying one of the most repeated monster scenes of the Archaic repertoire. Every ancient map of Greece silently carried her corpse, for the sanctuary's name, Pythô, preserves the verb for rotting — the dragon written into the geography itself.
